sitePublications.title: About Crossover
sitePublications.founderSummary: Jeff Kolyer is a former Silicon Valley technology founder who has lived in Stockton for more than a decade. Crossover grows out of his interest in the transition from work to vocation: how emerging technology, human attention, and local action can be directed toward unmet needs in the real world.

items.title: From work to vocation
items.body: AI and robotics are changing the relationship between work and survival. More of what people do today for wages may eventually be automated, accelerated, or made unnecessary. That raises a practical question: what should we do with greater freedom, capability, and time?
paragraphs: Crossover begins with one answer: turn toward real needs.

Instead of treating technology as an end in itself, Crossover explores how it can support a transition from compulsory work toward meaningful vocation: work chosen in response to reality, suffering, and unmet need.
This is an attempt to connect tools, attention, and action to the world as it is. The goal is to begin practicing a better future, not merely imagining one.

items.title: See clearly. Act locally.
items.body: Crossover Stockton is a public civic project based in Stockton, California. It starts with a gap: a need that is real, visible, and not being adequately met.
paragraphs: Stockton is where the founder has lived for more than a decade. It is a place where the project can meet people, visit institutions, and follow a need beyond what a website alone can show.

From there, we show up, look closely, learn from people involved, examine evidence, and take useful action. Understanding develops through observation, records, conversations, questions, and attempts to help.

The living feed is the outcome of that research: our current best account of the situation, not a list of activities. When evidence materially changes our understanding, we revise the account. Overview explains what is happening. Our work records what we have done and learned. What's next describes planned follow-up. Questions keeps uncertainty visible.
The collections in the left navigation—actions, activity, places, organizations, measurements, findings, and sources—hold the records and evidence behind the account.
We are trying to become informed in public. Before we can improve a situation, we have to understand it.

items.title: The work discovers the work.
items.body: Crossover does not begin with a master plan. It begins with attention to a specific need.
paragraphs: A record request may reveal a bottleneck. A field visit may expose a mistaken assumption. A conversation may uncover an existing effort. A small practical step may show what is possible, or what is missing.

The work discovers the work. We need enough contact with reality to take the next honest step, then let new evidence revise our understanding. A question may matter more than a conclusion, and the useful action may differ from the one we first imagined.
We make the process public: what we observed, what we found, what we tried, what remains unclear, and what might help next. The account can change as we learn.
We're building a system that continually revises its understanding of reality, and we discovered that system by continually revising our own understanding of what we were building.

items.title: A problem whose scale is unknown
items.body: Dogs are being abandoned and found roaming Stockton's streets. Some are lost pets. Others live with people experiencing homelessness and should not be assumed abandoned.
paragraphs: In April 2026, Stockton Street Dogs' founder estimated at least 200 to 300 dogs on Stockton's streets at a time, rising to about 400 during puppy season. In September, the group reported encountering three to ten dumped dogs a week, up from about one a week the previous year. These are the group's estimates and observations, not a verified count.

Stockton Animal Services recorded 3,106 stray-dog intake events in 2024 across its service area, which extends beyond Stockton. In October 2026, the shelter reportedly took in 828 animals, nearly 600 of them strays across species. Neither figure measures how many dogs are living on Stockton's streets now.
We still lack a verified count of dogs needing help, where they are, what condition they're in, and whether they're receiving care. The scale of the unmet need remains unknown.

items.title: Getting care isn't always straightforward
items.body: Finding a dog that needs help is one thing. Getting that dog into care can be another. Residents can report a stray to Stockton Animal Services, which operates the municipal shelter, but a report does not guarantee immediate collection or intake.
paragraphs: Animal Services says the shelter is regularly at capacity. Healthy strays generally need intake appointments; sick, injured, aggressive, and confirmed abandoned animals receive priority. That still does not tell us how quickly a particular dog receives care.

The city also describes a temporary found-animal foster pathway. Some residents can care for a found dog while shelter intake or adoption is arranged, and Animal Services may provide vaccinations and arrange sterilization. Not everyone can take an unfamiliar dog home.

Stockton Street Dogs feeds dogs in the field and invites people to foster, adopt, volunteer, or partner in rescue. Those routes depend on available people, funding, and places for dogs to go. Someone may report a dog and still have no immediate way to get it into care. How often that happens, how long dogs wait, and what ultimately happens to them remain unclear.

items.title: Capacity is expanding
items.body: Stockton is investing in more shelter space and veterinary services, although the effect on dogs needing help on the streets is not yet clear.
paragraphs: A roughly $10.5 million city shelter expansion is under construction. City plans include medical, isolation, and rehabilitation space; November 10 reporting also describes a new veterinary facility, adoption space, and a community resource center. The shelter now expects to open the expanded facility in spring 2027, later than the city's original fall 2026 target.

In June, the City Council approved a one-year extension of its Hard Luck Animal Welfare Advocates contract, up to $3.97 million, with four additional positions. Stockton Street Dogs has separately proposed a Canine Campus for shelter overflow and recovery and is seeking funds. We have not verified that the campus is fully funded, has a secured site, or has an opening date.
Construction, contracts, and proposals may expand care, but they do not yet show how many more dogs will receive timely help or whether the gap will close.

items.title: Reviewing the field-call records
items.body: Crossover received 7,183 Stockton Animal Services field-call records on November 2 and began reviewing them November 4. We are checking what each record says about a request, the response, and any recorded outcome, along with missing information and limits in the data. These calls cannot be counted as unique dogs or as the street population; findings from the review remain pending.

items.title: Getting closer to the problem
items.body: Crossover visited Stockton Animal Services, applied to volunteer there, asked about Doggie Day Out, and applied to volunteer with Stockton Street Dogs. These steps are ways to learn how care works in practice. The applications do not establish that we have participated or completed onboarding.

items.title: What can the records tell us?
items.body: First establish the calls' date range, categories, locations where recorded, and missing fields. Then examine recorded requests, response paths, and outcomes without treating a call as a dog or inferring an outcome the records do not contain.

items.title: How does a dog actually get help?
items.body: Follow up on the volunteer and Doggie Day Out inquiries, and ask care providers to describe the path from finding or reporting a dog to a response and possible care. Document what they confirm, where the path depends on capacity or eligibility, and where the answer remains unclear.

items.title: How many dogs currently need help on Stockton's streets?
items.body: No verified count exists. We need to distinguish dogs who are lost, abandoned, roaming, or living with people, and learn what help each actually needs. A dog seen on the street should not automatically be counted as abandoned or in need of removal.

items.title: What happens when someone reports a dog?
items.body: We want to trace the report, any recorded response or disposition, and whether the dog actually reached care. The field-call records may describe only part of that path; an administrative outcome does not by itself establish the dog's later condition.

items.title: Where does access to care break down?
items.body: Which services can accept a dog at the time someone asks? Capacity, cost, eligibility, and transportation may affect the answer, but we have not established how often each is a barrier in Stockton. Provider follow-up and the records review may clarify this.
